1.pericope_label: The charge of the sanctuary laid on Aaron and Levi

schools.summary: Calvin is the sharpest reader of the burden. Those bear the iniquity of the sanctuary who sustain the crime and the punishment of all its pollutions, as if God had said that negligence alone was tantamount to sacrilege; and from that severity he infers the dignity of the rites, since God would not so avenge the profaning of trifles, and something far more excellent must have been sought in these earthly elements. He applies the whole to pastors, on whom blame justly falls if religion is corrupted, doctrine impaired, or the people's welfare endangered. He also describes the arrangement as graded, the Levites ministering under the priests' hand at a degree half-way between them and the people, and draws from it both a lesson of reverence and a figure: if the holy seed of Abraham might not approach the typical sanctuary, how should we who were aliens penetrate to heaven unless a way were opened through Christ? The stranger forbidden here, he adds, is not the foreigner but everyone outside the tribe of Levi, so the line falls not between the Church and the nations but between the sanctuary's ministers and the people. Gill notices the pointed courtesy of the phrase the tribe of thy father, Amram having been a Levite, so that Aaron is told to reckon them brethren, which might conciliate their minds about his enjoyment of the priesthood; and he glosses their charge concretely as keeping out unfit persons and moving the tabernacle.

Henry reads the chapter as the answer to the last. The people had complained of the peril of drawing near, fearing the tabernacle in their midst would prove their terror rather than their glory; God replies through Aaron that the priests shall come near on their behalf, so that though the people keep their distance their communion is kept up by that interposition. He then turns the comfort into a warning: great honours had lately been heaped on Aaron, his rod having budded while the other princes' stayed dry, so God comes to remind him of the burden laid on him, that he may receive his office with reverence and holy trembling, and be not high-minded, but fear. The greater the trust committed to us, he adds, the greater the danger of contracting guilt by betraying it. He extends the iniquity borne to any duty of the sanctuary neglected or done out of season, and insists on the word chosen for the priests' own work: it is you shall serve, not you shall rule, since they were never meant to lord it over God's heritage, the priesthood being a service and ministers being servants.

Wesley says with Henry that the people are in good measure secured against their fears, and presses the equity of the burden, Aaron's dignity carrying his own sins and the people's to answer for, so none had cause to envy him. He takes the iniquity borne of suffering the punishment of every usurpation or pollution by Levites or people, the priests having power to keep them within bounds. Clarke points out the play on words, Levi coming from a root meaning to join, so the Levites shall be joined to the priests and perform the office conjointly, the priests principal and the Levites their associates.

Ellicott widens the iniquity borne beyond defilement by the transgressions of priests and people to the imperfections clinging to their services and offerings, and traces the verb behind Levi to Leah's speech at her third son's birth. Keil sets the section in its place: the laws given hitherto contained isolated stipulations but no comprehensive arrangement, and these instructions come to Aaron directly, only the tithe of the tithes being addressed to Moses as head of all Israel.

debates.question: What does bearing the iniquity of the sanctuary cover?

sides.position: the punishment of usurpations and pollutions by Levites or people which the priests had power to prevent
also the imperfections clinging to the priests’ own services and to the people’s offerings
the crime and punishment of every pollution, negligence alone being tantamount to sacrilege

themes: ye shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary
thy brethren the tribe of Levi, the tribe of thy father
they shall be joined unto thee
a stranger shall not come nigh unto you
I have given your priest’s office unto you as a service of gift

8.pericope_label: The priests' portion, the firstfruits and the firstborn

schools.summary: Calvin sees the grading of the tribe continued here, Aaron's family invested with peculiar honours while the other families of Levi are abased, the offerings of higher consecration going to the priests alone. He explains why the stated reason matters: the privilege comes by reason of the anointing lest the priests magnify themselves on the score of it, God's gratuitous liberality being meant to teach modesty, and the sons of Aaron obtained theirs by no right but that God was pleased to elect them, which is why it is called a gift. On eating in the sanctuary he reasons that the dignity of the holiest offerings would have been lessened had they been carried into private houses and mixed with common meats, and that God was unwilling to indulge the priests in sumptuous living, inducing them to frugality by the sight of the sanctuary. He denies that the estimation of the firstborn was the priests' to make: the phrase does not mean they prescribed the value but refers to the reckoning by which they were themselves bound, as appears from God naming the price immediately. On the covenant of salt he finds perpetuity expressed metaphorically, alluding to the sacrifices that might not be offered unseasoned, the figure implying inviolable stability, and God signifying that he is outraged himself if any man troubles the priests. Gill sharpens the wording about the firstling of a cow, a sheep or a goat: not to redeem them means not to take a price for them, since the creatures themselves fell to the priest.

Henry treats the section as a wage-bill. The priest's service is called a warfare, and who goes a warfare at his own charges? None shall serve God for nought; and from this provision the apostle infers that Christian churches must maintain their ministers, since those who served at the altar lived upon it, scandalous maintenance making scandalous ministers. Most of what they got came out of the sacrifices they themselves offered, so those charged with the offerings had the benefit, God's work being its own wages. The arrangement left them disentangled from worldly business, with no land to till and no cattle to tend, yet a more plentiful income than any family in Israel, so they might be entirely addicted to a ministry which requires a whole man; they lived from hand to mouth, that they might learn to take no thought for the morrow, and had no estates to leave their children, but left them to the care of the God who had fed them all their lives long. He marks the line between the most holy things and the lesser perquisites eaten at home by families that were clean, lets the causal sense of the anointing carry a doctrine, that nothing was given for personal merit but purely for the office, so all the comforts given to the Lord's people come by reason of the anointing they have received, and of the firstfruits draws the plain moral that we must serve God with the best, since he is the best, and is the first and must have the first ripe.

Wesley reads the maintenance as following on the office, and distinguishes the most holy things, eaten by priests alone in the sanctuary, from the rest. Clarke hears a rebuke in the pairing of man's firstborn with the firstling of unclean beasts, and describes the redemption as the Jews still practise it, the father sending at thirty days for a descendant of Aaron, who claims the child, takes gold and silver in exchange, and hands him back.

Ellicott prefers another construction of the reason given, rendering the words not by reason of the anointing but for an anointing portion, and the ordinance for ever as an eternal statute. He fixes the redemption price at five shekels for each firstborn not redeemed by the Levites.

debates.question: How should by reason of the anointing be rendered?

sides.position: causally, the portion following on the office and the anointing that conferred it
as a description of the portion itself, for an anointing portion, with an ordinance for ever as an eternal statute

debates.question: Did the priests fix the redemption estimate?

sides.position: the estimation was theirs to make, at the five shekels named
the phrase refers to the reckoning by which they were themselves bound, since God names the price immediately

themes: in the most holy place shalt thou eat it
all the best of the oil, and all the best of the wine
the firstborn of man shalt thou surely redeem

20.pericope_label: Levi has no inheritance, for the Lord is their portion

schools.summary: Calvin traces the tithe further back than Moses. The custom existed among the patriarchs, as Abraham and Jacob show, and the Apostle argues from it that Melchizedek's priesthood was superior, since when Abraham paid him tithes Levi paid too. Under the Law he finds two reasons: the land having been promised to Abraham's seed, the Levites were legitimate inheritors of a twelfth part, and were passed over when Joseph's posterity was divided into two tribes, so without other provision the distribution would have been unequal; and their labour in the sanctuary deserved remuneration, since men set apart for sacred offices should not be defrauded of their subsistence. God, who as King claimed the tithes by his own right, resigns them to the Levites and appoints them his representatives, which is what the clause about his being their inheritance means. He also reads the warning against approaching the tabernacle as aimed at the Levites' own diligence, since if the service of God were defiled even by inadvertency the crime would be imputed to them. Gill notices the arithmetic, the least of the tribes having the largest share of the land's increase without labour, the other nine parts being divided among all the rest at the charge of tilling them.

Henry states the exclusion and its reason together. The tribe was to have cities to dwell in but no ground to occupy, God intending them comfortably provided for but not over-rich, lest they think themselves above the work their wages obliged them to; as Israel was a peculiar people not numbered among the nations, so Levi was a peculiar tribe. The reason given is that God is himself their part, from which he infers that those who have him for their portion should look with holy contempt on this world's estates. Yet the Levites lived plentifully for all that, and he sets the paradox beside two others: the fowls reap not and yet are fed, the lilies spin not and yet are clothed, and the tribe without inheritance lived better than any in Israel. In the repetition of the arrangement he hears a deliberate balance, the Levites having the honour of attending the tabernacle, denied the Israelites, and the Israelites having inheritances in Canaan, denied the Levites, so each is kept from envying the other; and if ministers expect the people not to meddle with sacred offices, let them keep their own sphere and not entangle themselves in secular affairs.

Wesley gives three reasons for the exclusion: that they might be wholly devoted to God's service, that he had provided abundantly otherwise, and that dispersal among the tribes gave them better opportunity of teaching. Clarke prefers to measure. The Levites had the tenth of all produce, forty-eight cities and two thousand cubits of ground about each, which he reckons at fifty-three thousand acres; and since Canaan held about eleven million, their portion came to less than one part in two hundred and twelve. That is very small for a tribe which had consented to annihilate its political existence to wait on God's service, yet what they held was the best of the land, so a slender remuneration still left them independent.

Keil takes Aaron here as representing the whole priesthood, and holds that Jehovah was the portion not of the priests only but of the whole tribe, as Joshua says the priesthood of Jehovah was their heritage. Ellicott notes that Aaron is addressed as the priesthood's representative though he never entered Canaan, and carries the promise forward to all admitted into Christ's royal priesthood; of the warning against approaching the tabernacle he explains that bearing sin means bringing sin upon oneself and bearing its penalty, the primary sense from which the secondary one of bearing sin as atoning for it derives.

debates.question: What does the priesthood of Jehovah was their inheritance mean?

sides.position: that Jehovah himself is the portion of the whole tribe, the priesthood being his heritage
that it means the priesthood with its revenues, so the divine name stands for the gifts and tenths
holders: Knobel, reported and rejected by Keil

themes: thou shalt have no inheritance in their land
I am thy part and thine inheritance
I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel
lest they bear sin, and die

25.pericope_label: The Levites pay a tenth of the tenth

schools.summary: Calvin settles how many such payments there were. This is a second kind, a hundredth part of the whole produce, rendered by the tribe to Aaron's house; some reckon a third besides, but he will not agree, since it is improbable that a double levy fell in one year. A larger portion went to the priesthood, he adds, not merely as an honourable distinction but because greater integrity in spending was expected of them, and because they had peculiar burdens. He makes the comparison with threshing-floor and wine-press explicit: lest the tribe prove sordid, God declares their theft would be no less wicked in dealing dishonestly with Aaron's house than the nation's in withholding its own share, so the tenth of the tenth is reckoned as though it came from floor and press, and they stand no more exempt from the second levy than the people from the first. On quality he urges sincere liberality, that they set apart nothing lean or out of condition or in any way inferior, but whatever was most choice, which is the force of the word translated best, and literally the fat. Gill explains why the law comes through Moses, following Aben Ezra: it would not have been proper for Aaron to deliver an order in which he and his sons were so nearly concerned. He also sets out the tribe's liberty, that they were not tied to the tabernacle as the priests were with many holy things, nor to Jerusalem as the second levy was, but might eat at home.

Wesley reads the clause about the threshing-floor as acceptance rather than warning, since it is accepted of them as much as if offered out of their own lands and labours. Clarke observes what the law cost the tribe: having the tenth of the whole land, they had to render a tenth of that again, which considerably lessened their revenue, and the part rendered had to be picked from the best. Something of all must be given to God, he adds, as evidence of his goodness and of their dependence.

Ellicott states the pattern of the chapter as a rule: the law of the Levitical dues was given to Aaron and passed through him to the nation, while what the tribe owed the priesthood came to Moses and so to them. Working on the word rendered fulness, he notes that it is the term elsewhere given as the first of thy ripe fruits, used of grain fully ripe or of what the vine yields, so what they paid was reckoned as if it came off their own harvest; and he turns the clause about the remainder into a title of property, since what was left after the heave-offerings was as fully theirs as the corn and wine of any other Israelite. Keil describes the operation as a lifting off from everything received, of all the fat of it, that is of all the best, and supplies the reason for the limit on eating: they would load no sin upon themselves provided they lifted off the best and did not desecrate the holy gifts by eating in all kinds of places, which the earlier law forbade. He closes by setting the arrangement against the practice of the nations, where a heathen state with an hereditary priestly caste generally saw that caste rich and holding firm possession of the soil, as in Egypt, whereas Levi received no land at all but only towns to dwell in.

debates.question: How many kinds of tithe did the Law require?

sides.position: two, the people’s tenth and the Levites’ tenth of that
three, a further levy besides, which Calvin refuses as an improbable double payment in one year

debates.question: Where might the Levites eat what remained to them?

sides.position: in any place at all, clean or unclean, even a graveyard
in a clean place, be that where it would, which Gill prefers much better

themes: a tenth part of the tithe
as though it were the corn of the threshingfloor
the hallowed part thereof out of it
